keyVerseText: For before these days rose up Theudas, boasting himself to be somebody; to whom a number of men, about four hundred, joined themselves: who was slain; and all, as many as obeyed him, were scattered, and brought to nought. obeyed: or, believed
rootMeaning: The name Θευδᾶς (Theudâs) is of uncertain origin, with no clear etymological root provided. Abbott-Smith suggests it may be a contraction of Θεόδωρος (Theodoros), which means 'gift of God,' though this is not definitive. Without a known root, the name primarily functions as a proper noun identifying an individual, rather than conveying a specific meaning beyond that identity.
usageInScripture: Theudâs appears only once in Scripture, specifically in Acts 5:36, where it is translated simply as 'Theudas.' This singular occurrence limits the range of its use, firmly establishing it as a proper name referring to an Israelite figure. The consistent translation underscores its role as a historical person rather than a thematic or symbolic term.
theologicalSignificance: The mention of Theudâs in Scripture highlights the recurring pattern of false or misguided leaders who arise and attract followers but ultimately fail and are dispersed. Recognizing Theudâs as an Israelite who 'boasted himself to be somebody' serves as a sober reminder of the dangers of misplaced trust and human ambition apart from God's guidance. This underscores the Christian call to discern true leadership in Christ, who alone is the unshakable foundation. The name's uncertain origin also points to the humility needed in faith, focusing not on human titles but on God's sovereign purposes.
keyVerseReflection: Acts 5:36 recounts how 'before these days rose up Theudas, boasting himself to be somebody; to whom a number of men, about four hundred, joined themselves: who was slain; and all, as many as obeyed him, were scattered, and brought to nought.' Theudâs here represents a cautionary example of a self-proclaimed leader whose movement ended in failure and dispersion. The use of his name personalizes this warning, showing the real historical consequences of following those who claim status without divine authority.
